You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details:
- What the test sets up:
  - Two mutually exclusive option groups:
    - group1: options a, b
    - group2: options x, y
  - Command line arguments: ["-a"] → selects option a from group1.
  - Default properties: b=true (conflicts with a in group1), x=true (no conflict in group2).
  - Expected outcome: a is present, b is NOT present, x is present, y is NOT present.

- How parsing proceeds:
  1. Parser.parse(...) resets option state and group selections, then processes command line tokens.
  2. While processing "-a":
     - processOption(...) is invoked.
     - updateRequiredOptions(opt a) is called, which sets group1’s selected option to a (via OptionGroup.setSelected).
     - a is added to the CommandLine.
  3. After token processing, processProperties(properties) is called to apply defaults.

- The problematic logic in processProperties(Properties):
  - For each property, it checks only whether the CommandLine already has that specific option:
    - if (!cmd.hasOption(option)) { ... }
  - It then immediately prepares to add the option. There is even a comment hinting at the missing behavior:
// if the option is part of a group, check if another option of the group has been selected
    - This check is not implemented.
  - Crucially, it performs:
    - cmd.addOption(opt);
    - updateRequiredOptions(opt);
  - This order is wrong for grouped options:
    - When processing b=true:
      - b is added to the CommandLine first.
      - Only afterwards, updateRequiredOptions tries to mark b as selected in its group.
      - OptionGroup.setSelected detects that a is already selected and throws AlreadySelectedException.
      - Because the exception occurs after cmd.addOption(opt), the code either:
        - Ends up with an exception thrown (causing the test to fail), or
        - In earlier buggy behavior (per the issue description), left CommandLine containing both a and b because the group state wasn’t checked/updated at all.

- Why the test fails:
  - The parser should ignore b from properties because a (same group) was explicitly selected via the command line.
  - Instead, processProperties neither checks the group before adding b nor updates group state before adding. The check via updateRequiredOptions happens too late (after cmd.addOption), leading to an AlreadySelectedException or a conflicting state.
  - For x=true (group2), there is no conflict, so x is correctly added.

- Root cause:
  - Missing group-aware check and incorrect sequencing in Parser.processProperties(Properties):
    - It should:
      - Determine if the option belongs to a group.
      - If the group already has a selected option (different from the property option), skip adding the property option.
      - Otherwise, mark the group’s selection and then add the option.
    - Currently, it adds the option first and only then updates/validates the group, which is too late and causes the failure observed by the test.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
